title: Polycarp
hook: asked to curse Christ, the old bishop says he's served him eighty-six years and he's done no wrong

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius, and your line was god's wheat. What did you do for someone while you felt ground down? Today, an old man who had read Ignatius's letters. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

Soldiers arrive at a farmhouse outside Smyrna late in the evening. The man they've come for could have run again. He doesn't. He comes downstairs, talks with them, and, according to the account written by his church, orders food and drink set out for them, as much as they want. Then he asks one thing: time to pray. They give it, and he prays so long, and so fully, that some of the men who came to arrest him are sorry they came. His name is Polycarp. He is the bishop of Smyrna, and he is very old. Before long he'll be standing in the stadium.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a letter from his church, telling what happened. In the stadium the crowd is roaring. The Roman governor, the proconsul, is almost gentle. Have respect for your age, he says. Swear by the fortune of Caesar. Say: away with the atheists. That's what the crowd called Christians, because they wouldn't honor the gods. Polycarp looks up at the packed stands, waves his hand at the crowd, groans, looks to heaven, and says: away with the atheists. He says the words, and turns them around. The governor presses. Swear, and I'll let you go. Curse Christ. And Polycarp answers, in the line the church remembered: eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me? Some readers take eighty-six years as his age, others as the years since his baptism. Either way, it's a lifetime. The governor threatens wild beasts, then fire. Polycarp answers that the governor's fire burns for a little while and goes out. The account says the fire was lit around him, and in the end an executioner's dagger took his life. And then a very human detail: afterward his church gathered his bones and laid them somewhere safe, and planned to gather there to keep the day of his death as a birthday. Tradition says Polycarp had known John, the disciple of Jesus. That ties him to the story we've walked this week: Peter and Paul, Luke, the Didache, Clement's plea, Ignatius. Polycarp had even received a letter from Ignatius himself.

Here's the practice: name a long faithfulness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've been faithful to for years: a spouse, a friend, a parent, a child, a congregation, a promise. Count the years, roughly. Notice what those years held: the good, the dull, the hard. Then turn it around: who has been faithful to you for years? Hold both names. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them, and for whatever has kept you faithful. If you don't, simply let gratitude sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Polycarp. The old bishop of Smyrna who, told to curse Christ, said he had served him eighty-six years and had never been wronged.
Your line: eighty-six years. Today, tell the person you named that you've noticed their faithfulness, in one plain sentence. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Polycarp as a saint and martyr on his feast day, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp is read as an early example of Christians keeping the anniversary of a martyr's death.

original.note: Greek: away with the atheists, the cry the governor tells Polycarp to say (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9).

trapdoor: what you thought: Polycarp was a stern old martyr.
what it means: an old bishop who fed his captors, prayed, and turned the crowd's cry around before refusing to curse Christ.
what a scholar hears: the Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter from his church, keeps both the eighty-six years and the plan to remember his death as a birthday.
recall: let the exiles go home to build

notes: Editor pass: 'bound and burned' corrected to the account's fire and dagger (15–16); 'every year' and 'tomorrow morning' cut as not in the text; 'his life spans' Peter and Paul cut (a dating claim the text does not make); 'fire for an hour' softened to 'a little while'; second 'either way' removed.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is paraphrased throughout (Lightfoot's translation not verified word for word): retreat to a farm (5); food and drink for his captors, request for time to pray, some captors sorry (7); 'have respect to thine age', 'swear by the genius/fortune of Caesar', 'away with the atheists', 'fourscore and six years' (9); fire that burns for a season, or an hour (11); burned (15–16); bones gathered and the anniversary kept as a 'birthday' (18). Check each.
'Eighty-six years' is in the cited text (9). The note that readers aren't sure whether it is his age or years since baptism is a common observation; confirm.
'Tradition says Polycarp had known John' (Irenaeus 3.3.4; Eusebius 5.20); attributed to tradition.
'The account says he was bound and burned' simplifies ch. 15–16 (the fire forms an arch around him; he is finally killed with a dagger). A Keeper may prefer the fuller account.
'The crowd called Christians atheists, because they wouldn't honor the gods' is a historical gloss; the text (3, 9, 12) shows the cry. Confirm.
